newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh's Hasina pins big hopes on oil reserves.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh's Hasina pins big hopes on oil reserves.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said on Tuesday that every house could have electricity within three years if the poverty-stricken country could exploit untapped gas and oil.

"We have made several deals with foreign firms for exploration of oil and gas. If the works proceed all right, we will get huge energy. Our economy will change if we could utilise the energy in a planned manner," Hasina said at the opening of her Awami League party's two-day convention.
"The prospect of (finding a) huge quantity of natural gas has opened up scope for generating electricity...that it would be possible to reach electricity to every home in next two to three years.
"We don't want to remain poor. It's no prestige to be the leader of a poor nation," the prime minister said.
Bangladesh has proven reserves of 10 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, but the country faces a severe shortfall of electricity that often shuts industries and cuts domestic power supplies.
But Hasina said there was a "conspiracy against our development efforts", apparently referring to the opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) of her predecessor Begum Khaleda Zia.
"Remain vigilant against the conspirators," she said.
Hasina's call coincided with a BNP-led general strike which virtually paralysed 11 southeastern districts and the country's main port of Chittagong.
Police and witnesses said more than 50 people were injured in bomb blasts, clashes between rival activists and attack on a train at Feni, 100 km (65 miles) from Chittagong.
BNP, which lost to the Awami League in elections last year, said the strike was held in protest against repression of opposition activists and the government's "pro-Indian policies".
BNP leaders claim nearly 200 party workers and supporters have been killed in last 10 months, a charge the government has denied.
Hasina said she was determined to strengthen democratic values in the country, and vowed not to "allow anyone ever to use the army to attain personal ambition".
Army generals ruled the south Asian country for nearly 15 years after Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, Bangladesh's independence leader, was killed in the country's first coup in 1975.
